speaker_role: current admissions officer (Dean Z, University of Michigan Law School)
commercial_incentive: none evident; official law school admissions informational vlog
key_insights: For law school applications, the speaker recommends a mix of two academic and one professional recommender, or two professional and one academic, depending on how long the applicant has been out of school

Recommenders should know the applicant well enough to write more than a few generic sentences; a TA/graduate instructor from a small section can be a better choice than a famous professor who taught a 300-person lecture
Applicants should ask each recommender individually whether they feel comfortable writing a strong, detailed letter, giving them an explicit 'out' rather than asking multiple people simultaneously
It is not considered unethical for a recommender to ask the applicant to draft the letter, as long as the recommender still edits and personalizes it
Strong letters can meaningfully offset weaknesses elsewhere in an application, such as a lower GPA or standardized test score, per the speaker's own admissions experience
notable_or_distinctive: generic advice; off-scope for this undergraduate-admissions knowledge base since the speaker explicitly discusses JD/law school admissions (including 'K to JD' recommenders)
reliability_notes: OFF-SCOPE: this is graduate/law school admissions content (University of Michigan Law School admissions dean), not US undergraduate admissions, so relevance is marked low despite being a credible first-person admissions-officer account.
